the-name.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Μονόκερως**. Etymologically it means "'Single-horned' (from μόνος + κέρας)"[^1].

The ASCII form *monokeros* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Monókerōs** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same letter
- **o** → **o** — Same letter
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **o** → **ó** — Stress mark (acute/tone)
- **k** → **k** — Same letter
- **e** → **e** — Same letter
- **r** → **r** — Same letter
- **o** → **ō** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **s** → **s** — Same letter

Attested and derived spellings of the name:

- **Monokērōs** — macron-only form: LSJ convention: length only, no stress mark

The project holds the domain **monókerōs.com** (xn--monkers-n0a72f.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.
Aristotle, collected works, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 322 BCE.

overview.body:
**Monókerōs** (*monokeros*) — The Single Horn — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Purity, Rarity, Wonder". The name means "'Single-horned' (from μόνος + κέρας)"[^1].

Monókerōs begins not in myth but in the first travel writing of the West: Ktēsias' account of the wild asses of India, each bearing a single horn a cubit and a half long. Between his report and the medieval virgin-and-unicorn lies the whole history of how observation becomes symbol.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Monókerōs** and serves its temple at [monókerōs.com](https://xn--monkers-n0a72f.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *monokeros* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.
Aristotle, collected works, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 322 BCE.
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia, Loeb Classical Library, 77.

original-script.body: The name is written in Greek as **Μονόκερως**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *monokeros* and the PuniCodex restoration **Monókerōs** are measured: the restoration preserves both its pitch accent and its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

domains.body:
Monókerōs begins not in myth but in the first travel writing of the West: Ktēsias' account of the wild asses of India, each bearing a single horn a cubit and a half long. Between his report and the medieval virgin-and-unicorn lies the whole history of how observation becomes symbol.[^1]

### The Alicorn

The single horn, credited from antiquity with detecting and neutralizing poison.

### India

Ktēsias placed the one-horned wild asses in India — reports that likely fused rhinoceros, onager, and oryx.

### The Re'em

The Septuagint rendered the untamable Hebrew re'em as monokeros — the unicorn's biblical passport.

### The Untamable

In Job the re'em-monokeros is God's exhibit of what no man can bind to a furrow.

sources.citation: Aristotle, collected works, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 322 BCE.

symbols.body:
The iconography associated with Monókerōs concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The single horn** — Unity, sovereignty, and the single point of concentrated power
- **The wild ass** — The original Greek animal — swift, fierce, and uncatchable
- **The cup** — Alicorn drinking vessels of kings, supposedly proof against poison

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

syncretism.body:
The medieval West transformed the report into allegory: the Physiologos made the unicorn catchable only by a virgin, and Christological exegesis followed — the horn the single nature, the capture the Incarnation. Heraldry crowned the transformation: the unicorn, chained because a free one is dangerous, became the royal beast of Scotland and the supporter of the British royal arms, facing the lion.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

cultural-legacy.body: Narwhal tusks, sold as alicorns, were literally worth their weight in gold; the Danish throne was "made of unicorns," and Elizabeth I paid £10,000 for one. Today the unicorn is the emblem of rarity itself — from heraldry to finance's "unicorn" startup — while scholars read Ktēsias' beast as a composite memory of the rhinoceros, the onager, and the profile-view oryx of Indus seals.[^1]

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

archaeology.body: The unicorn's material trail begins with the Indus "unicorn" seal motif — thousands of steatite seals showing a one-horned bovid, almost certainly a bull in profile — and runs through Mesopotamian and Achaemenid art to the medieval narwhal-tusk trade. No ancient Greek depiction of Ktēsias' beast survives; the physical record is the trade itself: cups of "alicorn" in royal treasuries, like the one inventoried in the French crown jewels.[^1]

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

epithets.body:
The one-horned beast collected names in four languages.

- **ὁ Ἰνδικὸς ὄνος** — 'the Indian ass'; Ktēsias' original description, the report before the legend.
- **μονόκερως** — 'the single-horned'; the Greek zoological term, used soberly by Aristotle.
- **monoceros / unicornis** — the Latin continuations, Pliny's "fiercest animal."
- **re'em** — the Hebrew wild ox whose Septuagint translators chose monokeros, giving the beast its biblical career.
- **alicorn** — the medieval name for the horn itself, when the substance became more valuable than the animal.

sources.citation: Ctesias, Indika F45; Aristotle, History of Animals 499b; Pliny, NH 8.76.

mythology.body:
The Greek tradition is zoological, not mythological: no hero fights the monokeros, no god rides it. Its power lies precisely in being reported — a creature at the edge of the map, described by those who claim to have seen its horn in the flesh.[^1]

### Ktēsias of Knidos (The Report)

Ktēsias, physician to the Persian king Artaxerxēs, wrote in his Indika of Indian wild asses "swift as horses, with a single horn on the forehead, white at the base, black in the middle, crimson at the tip." Their horn shavings, he says, are an antidote to all poisons; their fleetness makes them unhuntable. His report is the unicorn's birth certificate.[^2]

### Aristotle's List (The Verification)

Aristotle, a more careful zoologist, lists in his History of Animals the solid-hooved, one-horned "Indian ass" alongside the oryx — and gets the mechanics right: a real single horn must grow from the skull's midline, unlike the paired horns of cattle. Pliny the Elder later repeats the monoceros as "the fiercest animal," catchable, he was told, only by stratagem.

### The Re'em Passage (The Translation)

When the Septuagint translators met the re'em — the wild ox of Hebrew scripture, image of untamable strength — they chose monokeros. The Latin Vulgate made it unicornis, and the King James Bible "unicorn": thus a Greek traveler's Indian ass entered the Psalms and Job, and every subsequent European imagination.

### The Virgin Stratagem (The Hunt)

The Physiologos — the early Christian bestiary — added the capture-scene that made the legend medieval: the unicorn, uncatchable by any hunter, will run to a virgin seated in the forest and fall asleep in her lap, where the hunters take it. The allegory wrote itself: the horn the single nature, the virgin Mary, the capture the Incarnation — and the Greek traveler's report became the Middle Ages' most painted animal, from the Unicorn Tapestries to the royal arms of Scotland.

sources.citation: Aristotle, collected works, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 322 BCE.
Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia, Loeb Classical Library, 77.

meditation.body:
Monókerōs is the patron of honest impossibility. The Greeks never claimed to rule it, saddle it, or even see it clearly — they only reported it, at the edge of the known. It stands for the single, the indivisible, the thing that cannot be made to serve: a reminder that some of the world's value lies in what refuses to be caught.

Perhaps that is why the unicorn survives every debunking: it was never a zoological claim but a standard of rarity. Ktēsias wrote down what he heard, the translators chose the word they had, the medievals made a theology of it, and the financiers made a valuation — each age reporting the beast it needs. The one horn points, in every century, at the same thing: the value of what cannot be bred, bound, or brought to market.[^1]

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.

homeric-hymns.body: No hymn addresses the monokeros, and the silence is diagnostic: the Greeks never made it a god or even a monster of the agonistic kind — it had no cult, no oracle, no adversary. Its "hymns" are the zoological chapters: Ktēsias' Indika, Aristotle's History of Animals, Pliny's Natural History, and the Septuagint's re'em passages. The absence from the hymnic corpus marks the boundary of Greek religion exactly: the one-horned beast belonged to report and wonder, not worship — a creature at the edge of the map, not of the altar.

sources.citation: Ctesias, Indika F45; Aristotle, HA 499b; Pliny, NH 8.76.

oracle-sites.body: The unicorn's stations are treasuries, not temples. The **French crown's** alicorn cups, inventoried through the Middle Ages, and the Danish coronation chair at **Rosenborg** — long believed to be of unicorn horn — are its reliquaries; the narwhal trade that supplied them ran through Arctic Norway and Iceland. Antiquity's only "site" is textual: the India of Ktēsias' Indika, the royal menageries of Persia where he claims the horn was seen. No sanctuary ever claimed the beast, which is the point: it was proof against capture, and so against cult.

sources.citation: Lavers, The Natural History of Unicorns (2009); Ctesias, Indika F45.

iconography.body: The iconography begins in paradox: the Indus "unicorn" seals — thousands of steatite stamps of a one-horned bovid, almost certainly a bull in profile — are the oldest candidate images. Greek art ignores the beast entirely; the medieval West made up for it: the **Unicorn Tapestries** (the Cloisters) and the *Lady and the Unicorn* series (Cluny) fixed the white horse-goat with the spiral horn, and Scottish heraldry crowned it in chains — "a free unicorn is a dangerous beast." Every image after Ktēsias is a portrait of a report, never of a sighting.

sources.citation: The Unicorn Tapestries (Metropolitan Museum); Indus seal corpora (CISI).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/mo.nó.kɛː.rɔːs/** — Attic Greek.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: mo-NO-keh-ross, stress on the antepenult with a long final ō.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — μονόκερως
- **Latin** — monoceros / unicornis
- **English** — unicorn
- **Owned form** — Monókerōs

Greek μονόκερως is a compound: mónos ("single") plus kéras ("horn"), stressed on the first element. Greek authors used it of real and reported animals alike — the rhinoceros included — centuries before Latin monoceros and the medieval unicorn softened it into legend.

sources.citation: Ctesias of Knidos, Indika, Photius, Bibliotheca epitome; ed. Bigwood, 398 BCE.
